chapters.title: Welcome Back — One Week Off in Taiwan

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Hi everyone. It's so wonderful to see you again. It feels like it's been almost way too long — it feels like it's been five or six months. And this is the one week I have off. We're doing a big preparation for a transmission in October, and I know a lot of you are already aware of that, and are already planning for it here. This is the one week I have off — kind of perfectly sandwiched and planned between everything else. Geshe Michael has another program at Dragonshead this week; 4,000 people around the world are choosing their branches. So instead of taking a nap, I just said, "just fly to Taiwan and spend some time with you."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I'm becoming more and more Chinese every day. My TCM doctor makes me wear these stupid socks. "It's good for you, Tim." Do you know how hard it is to sleep with socks on? But it seems to be helping. If I get uncomfortably hot, though, I'm just going to take them off, I'm sorry. I bought the coolest socks possible — coolest, like temperature-coolest. They're linen socks. I'm not sure if that counts. But I'm becoming more and more Chinese every day — maybe not in look, but in my head, my heart, in practicing and learning. I'm trying to learn.

chapters.title: Why Are We Doing Classics Course 8?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So Brian and I were talking about this today, actually. We were talking about how this course relates to the actual transmission that's coming up. Because I don't believe that anything happens for no reason at all. What's the secret message here? Why are we doing Classics Course 8? And notice we changed the name too — because we're transitioning to become the V Houses, so we've renamed these courses the Classics Courses.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: My question is, why Classics 8? Why are we getting this course right now? Is it because we did the seventh course back in March, and this is the next one? Logically, that would make sense: we did 7 before, dummy, so we're doing number 8 now. But as we're entering into a very different practice offered by Geshe Michael, he's asking us to look at the world a bit differently.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: How many people — this is your first time at an ACI course? Two people. Three people. We have three new people. Congratulations. Welcome. So when I say we're learning a different way of thinking, you don't even know what the other way of thinking is yet — so congratulations.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I like to think that everyone arrives at the right time, when they need to be here. It doesn't matter whether you've been here before or you're brand new — what you're going to hear is going to be important to you. So ask yourself: why is this seed opening up right now for me? What does it mean to ask, "what seed is opening up for me now?" Why am I here? Am I here because my friend brought me? Or because I heard about it online?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Ask yourself the question: why are you listening now? Why did now happen now? What causes in the past were planted by you that are ripening now, for you to be here in this classroom?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: By the way, I asked myself this question this afternoon. Brian and I found the best coffee in Taipei City. It's called Helen's Coffee. It's so expensive. But so good. And I was like, why do I get to experience this today? What seeds did I plant that ripened today for the best coffee I've ever had in Taipei City? It's only a 10-minute walk from here. And then — why is it expensive too? Why is the best coffee the most expensive? Because it's rare.

chapters.title: Rare and Expensive — Taking Apart Cause and Effect

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So here's a good question. Why do rare things have to cost more money? We're going to play a little game right now. Sorry, we're going on a trip — we're not even going to talk about ACI 8 right now. And I think it's important, especially for the new people, but also for you: really think about it. Is there a necessary relationship between things that are rare and things that are expensive? It seems like there might be.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Can we think of something that's rare and expensive?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Diamonds. Gold.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Diamonds, gold, rubies. They're rare, and they're expensive. Okay, that sounds pretty good, right? Now can you think of something that's expensive but not rare?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Houses.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There you go. Housing in Taiwan is very expensive. How many houses are there in Taiwan? Millions of them. That's a great example.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we have two so far: rare and expensive, and not rare but expensive. Now, what about not expensive but rare? This one might be a little harder. For example, another one around food: every year the Girl Scouts sell these cookies, just once a year. The cookies are rare — but they're not expensive at all. We don't have Girl Scouts in Taiwan; they have Boy Scouts here, not Girl Scouts. Well, that's not fair.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we have three options so far, right? Rare and expensive. Not rare, but expensive. Not expensive, but rare. What about something that's not expensive and not rare?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Air. Grass. Peanuts. Rice.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we just created four relationships. What does that say about the connection between the two things? mu-shi-mu-sum [MU BZHI MU GSUM] — which is Tibetan for "there is no relationship." If something looks like cause and effect... because we've just accepted that something rare is expensive. But if you can do all of those permutations, then in your mind you break apart what you thought was the causal relationship.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I know you're thinking, "why are we talking about logic right now, Tim? It's 7:22 on a Tuesday, why are you forcing me to use my brain?" Because we're going to be talking about things that we can't necessarily perceive directly. And if we can use our mind to analyze it, we can understand the way our mind tricks us into believing that things are one way, when they're actually the other. We thought that things that are rare are expensive. How is that spiritual? Why am I talking about this?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Why are we here today? How did you first get into ACI? Did you think you got here because your friend invited you? Or because ACI invited you? Or because Tim came, because I showed up — "I like that guy, he's kind of cool"? Right? But is that the reason you got here?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I'd like you to think about it a little differently. What really brought you here? What things did you do? What seeds were planted in the past that opened up, so that you could even be in this room? Just think for a minute about all the things that had to happen in a certain way for you to be sitting here right now. It's not just one thing. It's not just that you heard an advertisement. You had to drive here, or take a bus, or take a taxi — and then you had to get into the vehicle. All the things you had to do today, just to get here. And how many things in that process, if they'd changed just slightly, would have meant you couldn't be here today?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I mean — could the one time you were crying when you were six months old in the crib, and your mom came to give you a hug, be a cause for you to be here right now? What if she had ignored you for 30 minutes? Could that have totally changed things, so that you wouldn't be here right now?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This is the invitation to think a little bit differently. What really brought you here right now? And are those things just random — like your mom giving you a hug when you were crying? Or could they have been something that had a higher meaning? So this is the question: what really brought you here? And that's what this course is about.

chapters.title: The Course — Death and the Realms of Existence

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: It's called Death and the Realms of Existence. It's a big, heavy name. And this course is really about what brought you here.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: If you understand that the mind is a continuation of seeds ripening — what started this life for you? What is it that opened up your life? What started it?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: The previous life. Karma.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The death of your last life. Your life started with your previous death. Have you ever thought about that before? Everyone thinks that life started when you popped out of your mom. But did you ever think about what brought you — what started you — before that?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So that's the idea here. We're starting from a point of view of not now, but before. There was a string of causes before I was born; the power of that, the force of that, carried through into this next life. So what force propelled you into this life? And why this one, and not something else? Why didn't you pop out as a cat?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: By the way, I got a new cat last week — I'll share pictures. Because if you all remember, my other cat passed right before I came here. I'll tell you the beautiful story of the new cat later.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But why did you pop out as a human? Why did you pop out as a human in Taiwan? Why did you pop out as a human, male or female? Why did you pop out into a certain family — with a certain demographic, a certain amount of money, a certain kind of family? Do you think some people are just lucky and some people are just unlucky? That's what we think — especially when we feel unlucky, and we're insanely jealous of those people who got born into an amazing life automatically and didn't have to try. But did they actually have to try?
